title: The Any-Benefit Approach
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Dave Stuart Jr. names a common flaw in school decision-making, the any-benefit approach, which says a new strategy or initiative is worth adopting if anything good could come of it (borrowed from Newport's Deep Work). He argues it makes saying yes too easy and makes scarcity of time and resources inevitable. His alternative is a cost-benefit approach, illustrated with three cases: switching to standards-based grading, buying a data-warehousing system, and habitually checking email and news. In each, he asks whether the real costs in labor, training, maintenance and focus are worth the benefits. The move is to treat wiser decisions as first requiring us to recognize the any-benefit judgments that lead to unwise ones.
points: The any-benefit approach approves anything that could possibly help, which makes yes easy and guarantees scarcity of time and resources.
The cost-benefit approach asks whether the full costs, in confusion, PD, labor hours and maintenance, are worth the specific long-term benefit for students.
A data system that needs twenty hours of training may be too complicated to work at the all-staff level it requires.
Checking email and news twenty times a day trains the brain against the focused work that good curricula demand.
Balance and focus cannot survive wherever any-benefit decision-making reigns.
quotes: The any-benefit approach to decision-making says that if anything good can possibly come of a new strategy or lesson or unit or initiative, then it's worth using (Newport, Deep Work, p. 186). Unfortunately, this is often the approach we take to deciding whether The New Thing We Learned is worth giving a go — in our schools, in our classrooms, in our lives.
Instead of the any-benefit approach, which leads us to smilingly sign-up for decisions we really can't afford, the cost-benefit approach helps us ask the right questions.

There could be many benefits in switching to standards-based grading (or no grades at all), but the costs — in confusion, in PD, in labor hours — are steep. Is the switch really the best way to spend those costs toward the long-term flourishing of your kids and community?
Is it possible that a tool that requires twenty hours of training to learn how to use it is too complicated to be practical at the all-staff level it needs to be?

But is it possible that, by checking it twenty times a day, we're training our brains to avoid focusing? Are we inhibiting our ability to do the kind of deep, focused work that is most likely to produce the literacy- and knowledge-rich curricula our students need across the school day?
The first step to making wiser decisions is to see the paths we take to unwise ones. Many times, those paths are marked with any-benefit judgments.
